sentences.text: Enceladus is only 500 kilometers in diameter, but it is one of the most fascinating worlds in the Solar System.
From 4 cracks at the south pole called tiger stripes, hundreds of geysers spray water vapor and ice crystals into space.
Cassini flew through these plumes and found salt, organic molecules, and hydrogen; exactly the ingredients needed for life.
These ice grains feed Saturn's E ring; Enceladus orbits Saturn in 33 hours.
Its surface is as white as fresh snow, and it reflects nearly all of the sunlight.
Our final stop is Iapetus, one of the strangest moons in the Solar System: one half as white as snow, the other half as black as coal.
Because the same face always points forward in its orbit, it sweeps up dark dust from the outer rings; ice evaporates from the warmed dark regions and falls onto the bright side.
Right in the middle of its equator runs a mountain ridge 13 kilometers high and 1,300 kilometers long; this gives it the appearance of a walnut.
Three and a half million kilometers from Saturn, it completes one orbit in 79 days; it is the only large moon that can see the rings from above.
In 2013, Cassini looked back from Saturn's shadow and caught a pale blue dot beneath the rings: Earth.
That day, people all over the world who knew the picture was being taken stepped outside and waved at a machine looking back at them from one and a half billion kilometers away.
Our tour of Saturn has come to an end.
You recognize Mimas the moment you see it: the giant Herschel Crater gives it the appearance of the Death Star from Star Wars.
The crater is 130 kilometers wide; that is, one third of the moon's diameter.
If this collision had been a little more violent, Mimas would have been shattered to pieces.
When the small wobbles in its orbit were studied in 2024, a surprising result emerged: beneath the ice shell of this small moon that looks frozen, there may be a young ocean.
Now let's take a closer look at the rings: this giant disk is not actually a single structure; it is made of billions of pieces of ice, from microscopic dust to the size of a house.
Its width exceeds 280,000 kilometers, but seen from the edge it almost disappears: in most places its thickness is less than 10 meters.
To scale, it is even thinner than a sheet of paper.
The largest gap in between, the Cassini Division, is opened by the gravity of the small moon Mimas.
The rings are probably only a few hundred million years old, and they are slowly raining down onto the planet; they could disappear within 100 million years.
When Galileo turned his telescope to Saturn in 1610, he saw strange bulges on either side of the planet that he could not explain, and called them ears.
It took half a century to understand that they were a ring; even today they take our breath away as the most elegant sight in the Solar System.
Welcome to the tour of Saturn: the sixth planet from the Sun, a gas giant 9 times the size of Earth in diameter.
When we place a true-to-scale Earth beside it, even how wide the rings are becomes clear.
Its density is lower than that of water; this is unique for a planet.
At its equator, winds reach 1,800 kilometers per hour, and its day lasts only ten and a half hours.
The Cassini spacecraft studied this system for 13 years, from 2004 to 2017, and completed its mission by diving into the planet's atmosphere.
Titan is Saturn's largest moon and the only moon in the Solar System with a thick atmosphere.
It is one and a half times as large as our Moon; its nitrogen-dominated atmosphere is 50 percent denser than Earth's and hides the surface with an orange haze.
Let's look beneath the haze: on its surface there are lakes, rivers, and rains of liquid methane and ethane; at minus 180 degrees, water is as hard as rock.
In 2005 the Huygens probe landed on its surface and photographed a riverbed covered with ice pebbles.
NASA's nuclear-powered drone named Dragonfly will arrive here in 2034 and fly over the dunes.
